_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 9 Gravity and Friction. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The five teaching chapters follow LESSON["lecture"] in content/lesson-9.py part by part, in the lesson's own words and examples: the forcemeter with the apple (2 N), the shoe (3 N) and the big book (5 N), and the grams misconception; the ball let go, and the child on the Earth whose down points to the centre, on top and on the far side; the block that slows and stops; the same block pushed on ice (9 marks), smooth wood (6) and rough carpet (2), a fair test, and the misconception that ice has no friction; the table and the bar chart, and the misconception that the tallest bar is the most friction. The forcemeter, the gravity scene and the three friction tracks are the lesson's own drawings (ART.kit.forcemeterSvg, ART.scene gravity, ART.sim friction).
title: Gravity and Friction
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Know that forces can be measured with a forcemeter.
Know that gravity on Earth is a force that pulls towards the centre of the Earth.
Know that friction is a force created between surfaces when they move against each other and it makes this movement harder.
Describe how smooth and rough surfaces can generate different amounts of friction.
Present and interpret results using tables and bar charts.

beats.say: Gravity is a force. It pulls things down, and keeps us on the ground.
Friction is a force too. It makes moving harder.
A forcemeter measures a force. It is a spring with a hook.
Hang an apple on it. Gravity pulls it down, and the spring stretches.
The scale tells you the force in newtons. This one reads two newtons.
Hang the shoe: three newtons. Hang the big book: five newtons.
The heavier the thing, the harder gravity pulls it, and the further the spring stretches.
A forcemeter does not measure grams. It measures the pull, in newtons. The pull is gravity.
Let go of a ball and it falls. Nobody pushed it. Gravity pulled it.
Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.
That is what down means. Down is towards the centre.
On the other side of the world, down points the other way.

at.side: the other side of the world

beats.say: The child there is not upside down. Wherever you stand, down points to the centre.
Push a block along the floor. It slows down, and then it stops.
What made it slow down and stop? Friction did that.
Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub together.
It pushes back on the moving block. It makes moving harder.
Rough surfaces make more friction. Smooth surfaces make less.
Push a block on ice, on smooth wood and on rough carpet.
Same block, same push. Only the surface changes: a fair test.
On the ice it slides a long way: nine marks.
On the wood, six marks. On the carpet it stops soonest: only two.
Even ice has a little friction. The block still slows down and stops.
Write your three distances in a table: ice nine, wood six, carpet two.
Then draw them as bars against a scale. That is a bar chart.
The scale up the side counts the marks: one, two, three, up to nine.
The tallest bar is the longest slide. That means the least friction.
Read the bars, and you see the pattern: smoother surface, longer slide.
A forcemeter measures a force. It reads the pull in newtons.
Gravity pulls things down, towards the centre of the Earth.
Friction makes moving harder. Rough surfaces make more of it.
A bar chart shows the pattern at a glance: smoother surface, longer slide.
